# Cartridge: system and authoring guide

Cartridge hosts replaceable Lua and SDK process cartridges. Start with
`cartridge help`: every document the host and each cartridge carry, as one tree
of modules, documents and sections. `cartridge help <id>` lists a module's
documents with their addresses, `cartridge help <id>/<file>[#<section>]` prints
one, `cartridge help <words>` prints every matching line with its address, and
`--json` gives the same as data. The manual is read from the cartridges
present, so it is never stale and never describes one cartridge from inside
another. Then read the linked plain-text guides relevant to the task. Paths are
relative to this source repository.

- [Writing good modules](docs/writing-good-modules.txt): useful events, direct
  integration, cartridge dependencies, and documentation through memo tools.
- [System architecture](docs/architecture.txt): repository layout, runtime,
  dependency resolution, processes, replacement, permissions, and cartridge roles.
- [Creating cartridges](docs/creating-cartridges.txt): complete Lua example,
  Rust SDK adapter, manifest fields, registration, profiles, and validation.
- [Development and operation](docs/development.txt): build/test selection,
  proxy, MCP registration, local data, Git workflow, and troubleshooting.
- [Memos and knowledge](docs/memos.txt): record types, validated writes,
  discovery, system prompts, and the cartridge-creation routine.
- [Settings](docs/settings.txt): how a cartridge contributes configuration
  keys, the three layers that settle them, and `cartridge settings`.

The executable declaration belongs in each cartridge.json. It includes purpose,
services, dependencies, grants, documented command argument arrays, and the
configuration keys the cartridge contributes. Reading commands does not execute
them. Memos hold context, decisions, and procedures. There is no separate
development JSON.

Every tunable value is a declared setting, never a constant. A cartridge names
its keys in `settings` with a type, a default, optional bounds and one line of
documentation; the host fills each one, checks it, and hands the cartridge a
complete configuration. That document is the only place the numbers live: a
cartridge carries no `Default` restating them, no `#[serde(default)]` on a
configuration field, and no second ceiling in code. It embeds its own
`cartridge.json` and reads the declared table back for an unhosted run, so the
values a test exercises are the values it ships. The host's own keys live in
`settings.json` beside this file, in the same shape. Three
layers settle a key — the declaration, then `~/.cartridge/config.lua` for this
machine, then the project's `.cartridge/config.lua` — each laid over the last
field by field. `cartridge settings` prints every key with its value and the
file that settled it, `--template` prints the whole surface as a config.lua
ready to save, and a non-zero exit means a cartridge is configured with a key it
never declared. Do not re-check in code a bound the declaration already states,
and do not pin a limit in a project file merely to restate its default.

Defaults are deliberately generous: a limit here exists to stop a runaway, not
to ration the machine. When one is in the way, raise the declaration rather than
working around it.

A cartridge brings its own surface. Its services, tools, settings, tests,
documentation and `.cartridge/help.md` page live in its directory and register
into the host; nothing about it lives anywhere else. It reaches another
cartridge in exactly two ways: through a key it declares in `needs` (a hard
dependency, which the host refuses to start without) or by listening to an
event another cartridge emits and reacting. It never carries another
cartridge's protocol for an optional feature, never names a sibling it did not
declare, and never installs a rule about a sibling into a shared cartridge.
Installing or uninstalling a cartridge therefore changes nothing outside it.
`just isolation` checks every cartridge against this rule.

A good cartridge owns a concrete capability, exposes useful state changes as
events, and calls declared dependencies directly for required results. Preserve
the host's context, errors, and lifecycle. Keep service and event contracts
discoverable in memos alongside the implementation.

The guides describe this checkout, not a promise that unfinished sandbox work
is complete. Source contracts and tests are authoritative when behavior changes.
See src/loader/document.rs for the manifest schema and src/settings/ for the settings
format and the host's own keys.
